student_profile.student_background: Practicing healthcare professionals across roles — clinicians, nurses, allied health staff, administrators, and researchers — non-technical, no programming assumed. The audience spans the three levels of the organization's AI taxonomy, and a single course serves all three: Operators (limited end-user interaction with the AI; need to accurately interpret outputs and ensure the technology enhances rather than replaces judgement); Contributors (interact with the AI but do not make decisions about the technology); and Shapers (interact with the AI and hold decision-making capacity).
student_profile.aggregate_academic_performance: Experienced adult professionals with strong domain readiness; mixed comfort and confidence with AI tools.
student_profile.anticipated_learner_needs_and_barriers: Wide variation in AI fluency; assume little formal AI training. Learners engage best with REAL, concrete material — actual clinical risk scores, published studies, documented device cases — not abstract principles. Plain language, terms defined on first use, short daily sessions.

instructor_preferences.instructor_emphasis_intent: This module teaches the pros and cons of AI assistants in diagnosis and patient management through REAL, VERIFIABLE material. Named tools, published studies, real device cases, and validated clinical scores ARE allowed and encouraged — but every named fact, number, and example MUST come from the provided source excerpts; never invent or embellish an example, statistic, or citation. When citing a named study, score, tool, or report, include its source URL from the excerpts on the slide. Cover the benefits (pros) and the risks and limitations (cons) with equal seriousness, and give substantive treatment to safety, trustworthiness, validation, and explainability. Address what the Operator, the Contributor, and the Shaper each need to interpret, do, and decide.
instructor_preferences.instructor_style_preferences: Visual-first, punchy slides modeled on the client's own decks — NEVER walls of bullets. Most slides carry ONE idea in at most 30 words of body text: a big statement, a short quoted dialogue, a figure with a two-line explanation, or a compact table. Directly under each frame title, put a one-line italic message stating the slide's takeaway (like 'AI helps at most stages — but the physician owns the final diagnosis'). When a figure from the source excerpts fits the slide, the figure DOMINATES the slide (most of its width) with at most two short lines of text beside or below it. The lecture script carries the depth and nuance; the slides carry the punch. Open every session with a real hook from the sources; one discussion-cases slide per session; light humor welcome.
instructor_preferences.instructor_focus_for_assessment: Assess judgment: scenario analysis, pros-and-cons reasoning, and when to trust, verify, or escalate an AI suggestion. No exams, no coding.

course_structure.course_learning_outcomes: Explain in plain language how AI assistants support diagnosis, clinical decisions, and patient management, using real documented examples; weigh the benefits against the risks and limitations, grounded in published evidence (validated risk scores, external-validation studies, real adverse-event reports); apply safety, trustworthiness, validation, and explainability to judge whether and how far to trust an AI output; keep clinical judgment central — AI supports, clinicians decide; and understand what the Operator, Contributor, and Shaper each must know and decide.
course_structure.weekly_schedule_outline: AI Assistants for Diagnosis and Patient Management: Session 1 — what the real record shows, taught one case at a time with patient scenarios throughout: the PESI risk calculator (what validated decision support looks like, built criterion by criterion); the Epic sepsis prediction model as the central before-and-after story — how sepsis recognition worked before the tool, what changed after deployment, and the documented impact of its errors (the Michigan Medicine news release and the JAMA external-validation record); the TruDi navigation system's launch claims versus its FDA MAUDE adverse-event reports; and the 2015 pigeon pathology study for what pattern recognition is and is not — regulatory guidance appears only as brief support in this session, never as its subject; Session 2 — validation in depth; Session 3 — device safety in depth; Session 4 — image classifiers in depth; Session 5 — governance (FDA GMLP, CDS guidance, transparency principles, change control, the Action Plan); with safety, trustworthiness, validation, and explainability applied throughout, and the Operator, Contributor, and Shaper roles addressed in every session

assessment_design.assessment_format_preferences: No exams and no coding. Scenario Judgment (40%) — work real-material scenarios (an AI risk flag disagrees with clinical impression; an alert fires on a patient who looks fine) and justify trust, verification, and escalation decisions. Pros-and-Cons Analysis (35%) — for AI in diagnosis and patient management, argue both sides from the evidence. Discussion participation (25%) — engage the no-clean-answer cases.
assessment_design.assessment_delivery_constraints: Short applied deliverables submitted via the learning platform.

teaching_constraints.platform_policy_constraints: Institution-approved learning platform; accessibility standards; no patient-identifiable information. Named tools, studies, and device cases are permitted when drawn from the provided public sources with attribution.
teaching_constraints.ta_support_availability: Facilitator-led or self-paced; no teaching assistant assumed.
teaching_constraints.instructional_delivery_context: Professional development delivered as ~1-hour daily sessions; this demo module spans 5-6 such sessions built around real cases, vignettes, and discussion.

institutional_requirements.program_learning_outcomes: Aligns with the digital-education program's goals for responsible AI adoption and sound clinical judgment about AI.
institutional_requirements.academic_policies_and_institutional_stan: All named examples, statistics, and cases must be traceable to the provided public sources (attribution on slide); no fabricated content; no patient-identifiable information; clinical-ethics norms respected.
institutional_requirements.department_syllabus_requirements: Module must include learning outcomes, session structure, the assessment approach, and a sources page listing every cited source with its URL.

prior_feedback.historical_course_evaluation_results: Revision of an earlier draft. Client feedback on the previous version: too generic and not engaging — needs real named examples (real risk calculators, published studies, documented device cases) with sources shown, patient vignettes, discussion cases, and workflow tables, in the style of the client's own course materials; one module only for this demo; every fact grounded in real sources with no false information.

session_structure: Each chapter of this course IS one one-hour session, and its deck must stay a lean, self-contained hour: open with the session's real hook from the sources, close with a short knowledge check, and keep the deck to roughly 12-16 slides. The session must be built AROUND applied material — patient scenarios, worked examples from the source's own numbers, a where-AI-fits workflow slide, and discussion cases — with at most a third of the slides being conceptual explanation. Do NOT sub-divide a chapter into further sessions and do NOT re-teach material that belongs to another session.
engagement_style: THE VERY FIRST CONTENT SLIDE after the title must BE a real hook — the pigeon study or the real news headline — never a definition, framework, or guidance summary. Teach through REAL material with ONE THING PER SLIDE — every slide holds exactly one story, one example, one image, one table, or one question, sized to fill the page; never combine two ideas on a slide and never crowd a slide: (1) PATIENT SCENARIOS are the backbone — include 4-5 of them, each on its OWN full slide, each a DIFFERENT patient context drawn from the session's sources, in exactly this format: patient facts (2 short bullets), a block titled 'AI says' with one quoted line, a block titled 'Physician thinks' with one or two quoted lines, a one-line takeaway. Nothing else on that slide. (2) WORKED EXAMPLES — include 2, each spanning its own slide or two: a risk score built criterion by criterion from the documented criteria, and a study's own reported numbers unpacked step by step. (3) BEFORE AI / AFTER AI / IMPACT arc — for the session's central system, one slide on how the task worked BEFORE the AI tool (as the sources describe it), one slide on what changed AFTER deployment, and one slide on the IMPACT OF THE ERRORS (what the documented false alarms and misses cost in practice). Each its own slide, each grounded in the excerpts. (4) NEWS AS STORY — tell the real news story with its headline, date, people, direct quotes, and numbers; one story beat per slide; set up a question on one slide and reveal the key number on the NEXT. (5) One 'Where AI Fits in the Diagnostic Workflow' TABLE slide: rows = workflow stages, a verdict column with short colored chips (rendered with the LaTeX colorbox command: light-green Yes, light-yellow Limited, light-blue Physician), and a short example column. (6) One DISCUSSION CASES slide: 4-5 numbered one-line judgment scenarios with no clean answer. (7) One 'What Would You Do?' decision slide: a concrete moment, options A / B / C, considerations on the NEXT slide. (8) CLOSE with a KNOWLEDGE CHECK slide of exactly 3 short questions — questions ONLY, no answers on that slide. (9) At most 4 purely conceptual slides in the whole deck; keep body text short (a slide is mostly its one story/example/image); when a slide cites a named study, score, tool, report, or news story, put its SOURCE URL from the excerpts at the bottom; when a figure appears in the retrieved excerpts give it its OWN slide (0.75+ textwidth, two short lines max); NEVER invent a named example, number, quote, or citation — if it is not in the excerpts, teach it generically or leave it out. GOVERNANCE CAP: FDA guidance documents (change control plans, monitoring frameworks, labeling) may appear on AT MOST ONE short supporting slide in this session — the full governance treatment belongs to a later session; this session is the real cases. LENGTH: the deck holds 24-30 slides total; exactly ONE Learning Objectives slide and ONE Key Takeaways slide; each case gets at most 5 slides and no two slides may restate the same point. REGISTER: the audience is practicing clinicians and healthcare staff — address them as clinicians; never use the words 'students' or 'textbook' on any slide. TONE: this deck must FEEL like a story being told, never a briefing. Slide titles are active and curiosity-driven, like headlines ('The tool said sepsis. The patient said otherwise.') — never bureaucratic ('Framework for post-market considerations'). Light humor and punchy contrast are welcome. If a slide would read as generic advice that could appear in any AI course, cut it or replace it with the real case detail that makes the point. VISUALS: use ONLY the real figures present in the retrieved excerpts (photos, panels, charts from the sources) — give them their own slides; do not describe or invent any other imagery.
